claims.text: Phase stability in near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys is governed by a balance between entropy-driven random mixing and local chemical short-range order.
Specific elemental pair interactions induce short-range order in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Al and Ni tend to cluster and form nascent ordered regions in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Al–Ni short-range order promotes or modulates the formation of secondary B2-type ordered regions within a disordered matrix.
A mixed microstructure containing ordered regions in a disordered matrix can retain high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
The initial near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy has a predominantly disordered, single-phase structure.
Changing heat-treatment duration and cooling rate can controllably promote or suppress local Al–Ni clustering.
Al–Ni-enriched clusters nucleate ordered B2-type regions within the disordered matrix.
Attractive mixing enthalpies between specific elemental pairs drive Al–Ni clustering.
Pair clustering creates nanometer-sized short-range-ordered regions.
Short-range-ordered regions act as fine-scale precipitates or alter matrix free energy, thereby stabilizing a mixed-phase state.
The disordered matrix supplies toughness and radiation tolerance.
Processing that enhances short-range order will increase the amount of nanoscale ordered material relative to a quenched, disordered baseline.
Enhanced short-range order will improve high-temperature strength relative to the fully disordered baseline.
Enhanced short-range order will improve environmental resistance relative to the fully disordered baseline.
Samples with enhanced short-range order will retain radiation tolerance and cryogenic toughness because sufficient disordered matrix remains.
The proposed mechanism is limited to near-equiatomic compositions and processing conditions that avoid full long-range ordering or gross phase separation.
